questions.prompt: Which OOP concept allows a single interface to be backed by different implementations chosen at run time?

options.text: Encapsulation
Abstraction
Polymorphism
Composition

questions.explanation: Dynamic dispatch selects the implementation from the object's actual type, so calling code depends only on the interface. This is what makes substituting one subtype for another possible.

options.text: It hides internal state behind a controlled interface, so invariants cannot be broken from outside
It makes all methods static
It removes the need for constructors
It lets a class inherit behaviour from several parents

questions.explanation: By exposing only methods, a type can guarantee its own consistency. Anyone able to write the fields directly could put the object into a state its methods assume is impossible.

questions.prompt: In call by value, what does a function receive?

options.text: An unevaluated expression re-evaluated on each use
The address of the caller's variable
A copy of the argument's value
A reference that can rebind the caller's variable

questions.explanation: Because the callee works on a copy, assignments to the parameter are invisible to the caller. Call by reference passes the location instead, and call by name re-evaluates the expression at each use.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes static (lexical) scoping from dynamic scoping?

options.text: Static scoping resolves names by where the code is written; dynamic scoping by who called it
Static scoping resolves names by the call stack at run time
They differ only in performance, never in results
Dynamic scoping is resolved entirely at compile time

questions.explanation: Lexical scoping lets you determine a variable's binding by reading the surrounding source, which is why nearly all modern languages use it. Dynamic scoping makes the binding depend on the runtime call chain.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between overloading and overriding?

options.text: Both require the methods to be static
Overloading defines several methods with the same name but different parameters; overriding replaces an inherited method
Both are resolved at run time
Overloading replaces an inherited method; overriding varies the parameter list

questions.explanation: Overloading is normally settled at compile time by argument types, while overriding is resolved at run time by the object's actual class — which is why only overriding gives polymorphic behaviour.

questions.prompt: Where are local variables of a function typically allocated?

options.text: The data segment
The code segment
The stack
The heap

questions.explanation: Each call pushes an activation record holding parameters, locals and the return address, and popping it on return reclaims them automatically. Objects that must outlive the call go on the heap instead.

questions.prompt: What is a memory leak in a language without garbage collection?

options.text: Freeing the same pointer twice
Allocated memory that is never freed and can no longer be reached
Reading memory that was never initialised
Writing past the end of an allocated buffer

questions.explanation: The allocation stays reserved for the process lifetime even though nothing can use it, so a long-running program creeps upward in memory. The other options describe distinct bugs with their own symptoms.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a function to be recursive?

options.text: It has no side effects
It calls itself, directly or indirectly, on a smaller subproblem
It is compiled into a loop automatically
It can be called from several threads at once

questions.explanation: A correct recursion needs a base case and progress toward it; without both it runs until the stack is exhausted. Being callable concurrently is reentrancy, which is a separate property.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between an abstract class and an interface (or protocol)?

options.text: Neither can declare methods
Interfaces can only be used with primitive types
An interface can hold state and implementations; an abstract class cannot
An abstract class may provide state and partial implementation; an interface primarily declares a contract

questions.explanation: An abstract class shares code with its subclasses but usually restricts a type to one parent. An interface describes capability, so an unrelated type can adopt it without inheriting anything.

questions.prompt: Why is a compiled language typically faster at run time than an interpreted one?

options.text: Compiled languages have simpler syntax
Compiled programs never need an operating system
Interpreters cannot use the CPU cache
Translation to machine code happens once ahead of time rather than during execution

questions.explanation: The interpreter pays translation and dispatch cost on every execution, and has less opportunity for whole-program optimisation. JIT compilation narrows the gap by compiling hot paths at run time.
